title: Saltwater Intrusion
subtitle: Data Visualization Assignment 1 · filtering + plotting
story: You're a field hydrologist on Dr Kamaka's team at the University of Hawai'i. This afternoon, you're practicing your data analysis skills in the jungle lab. Later, you're expected to make your rounds testing sulfate across a series of wells, then meet a colleague at the beach to help them with their analysis. Let's hope nothing unexpected happens!

done.title: Congratulations!
done.body: You went from practicing data analysis in the jungle lab to verifying safe sulfate levels and discovering a salt water intrusion. Good work! Now you need to open the control panel and disconnect this well from the island's water system to prevent sea water from contaminating more fresh water.

rooms.title: The Honolulu field lab
rooms.debrief: You started with the grammar of a plot: map abundance against analyte for one aquifer and let the tallest bar name itself. Before you filter or threshold anything, you have to be able to read a chart — which axis is which, and what “highest” looks like on it.
rooms.technique: plot grammar — abundance x analyte (no filter)

question.prompt: Narrow to the aquifer_1 wells. Within aquifer_1, which analyte reaches the highest abundance?

feedback.correct: Correct — noted in your field notebook: within aquifer_1, dissolved_solids runs the highest, into the hundreds (up to ~340).
wrong: Keep only the rows where aquifer_code is "aquifer_1", then plot analyte against abundance and see which analyte sits far above the rest.
Chloride climbs past 100 within aquifer_1, but only one analyte reaches the many-hundreds.
You want the analyte whose whole spread sits highest inside aquifer_1, not just one high reading — which one?

hotspots.label: A pinned note
hotspots.body:
A pinned up note says: In order to spot anything unusual in a well's water supply, good data are needed: a broad survey that measures many analytes across many wells. That’s what this dataset is — but a survey this wide is unwieldy all at once. The first practical move is to narrow it down: filter to the slice you’re actually working — here, a single aquifer — and read within it. Filtering to the rows you care about, then plotting, is the workhorse of the whole survey.

These data are in long format: one row per well per analyte — 954 rows in all (106 wells × 9 analytes), though some readings come back blank (NA). There are 10 aquifer codes (aquifer_1…aquifer_10) and 9 analytes (Ca, Cl, HCO3, K, Mg, Na, SiO2, SO4, dissolved_solids). So a single well shows up on nine rows, one per analyte.

tibble [954 x 6] (S3: tbl_df/tbl/data.frame) $ aquifer_code: chr [1:954] "aquifer_1" "aquifer_1" "aquifer_1" ... $ well_name : chr [1:954] "Alewa_Heights_Spring" "Alewa_Heights_Spring" ... $ longitude : num [1:954] NA NA NA NA ... $ latitude : num [1:954] NA NA NA NA ... $ analyte : chr [1:954] "SiO2" "Cl" "Mg" "Na" ... $ abundance : num [1:954] 11 20 7.6 14 0.6 7 ...

hotspots.label: Staring off gives an idea
hotspots.body:
Why sulfate? Sulfate (SO4) is a farmland watch-marker: fertiliser and irrigation return-flow push it up, so a well trending high in sulfate can signal agricultural influence on the groundwater. Field teams carry a watch line — a value that doesn’t mean danger, just ‘keep an eye on this one’. On a round you find the highest reading in the aquifer you’re walking and see which side of that line it sits on.

The survey is in long format: one row per well per analyte — 954 rows in all (106 wells × 9 analytes), though some readings come back blank (NA). There are 10 aquifer codes (aquifer_1…aquifer_10) and 9 analytes (Ca, Cl, HCO3, K, Mg, Na, SiO2, SO4, dissolved_solids). So a single well shows up on nine rows, one per analyte.

tibble [954 x 6] (S3: tbl_df/tbl/data.frame)
 $ aquifer_code: chr [1:954] "aquifer_1" "aquifer_1" "aquifer_1" ...
 $ well_name   : chr [1:954] "Alewa_Heights_Spring" "Alewa_Heights_Spring" ...
 $ longitude   : num [1:954] NA NA NA NA ...
 $ latitude    : num [1:954] NA NA NA NA ...
 $ analyte     : chr [1:954] "SiO2" "Cl" "Mg" "Na" ...
 $ abundance   : num [1:954] 11 20 7.6 14 0.6 7 ...

rooms.title: The Ke'ei coast wellhead
rooms.debrief: Now the filtering gained a threshold. You pulled the chloride readings for one aquifer and asked a yes/no question of a line: does any well cross the 250 mg/L alarm? Reading data against a fixed standard — over or under — is how a number becomes a decision.
rooms.technique: filter() aquifer + analyte, apply a threshold

hotspots.label: The colleague's laptop
hotspots.starterCode:
# your colleague's chloride check — it won't run. fix it, then find the answer.
hawaii_aquifers %>%
  filter(aquifer_code = "aquifer_6", analyte = Cl) %>%
  filter(abundance > 250)

check.prompt: Your colleague's chloride code is broken and won't run. Fix it, then find the one aquifer_6 well whose chloride crosses the 250 mg/L alarm line, and assign that well's name — exactly as it appears in well_name — to an object called answer. The click "Check my answer".
check.hint: The two = should each be ==, and Cl needs quotes: filter(aquifer_code == "aquifer_6", analyte == "Cl"). Then keep abundance > 250 and read off the well_name.

feedback.correct: Correct — noted in your field notebook: KEEI_B's chloride is 280 mg/L, the only aquifer_6 well over the 250 alarm line — a possible seawater intrusion. Time to check the sodium.
wrong: Fix the pipeline first — filter(aquifer_code == "aquifer_6", analyte == "Cl") — then keep the wells with abundance > 250 and read off the well_name.
Only one aquifer_6 well clears 250; the next-highest chloride sits at 210, safely under the line.
Assign the flagged well's exact well_name to answer — mind the spelling and capitals.

entry.title: Down to the coast
entry.text: Aquifer 1 checks out — its highest sulfate well sits under the watch line. You follow the trail downhill, out of the jungle and onto the shore, where a colleague is waiting at the Ke‘ei wellhead. They're mid-survey on Aquifer 6 and out of time. They push their chloride data into your hands. “Please can you analyze these data quick?” they ask. “I have to head out, but if any well's chloride is over 250, that's a possible seawater intrusion — and if it is, check the sodium too.” Then they're off up the trail, so now it's just you and the numbers.

rooms.title: Down inside the Ke'ei well
rooms.debrief: The verdict. You filtered down to the one flagged well and tested a second line — sodium over 150 — and the two thresholds together spelled saltwater intrusion. That is the whole lesson in one move: narrow to the case that matters, test it against the standards, and let the data deliver the diagnosis.
rooms.technique: filter to the flagged well, second-threshold verdict

question.prompt: KEEI_B’s chloride is already over 250. Now check its sodium. Is sodium above the 150 mg/L line — and what does that mean?
options: Na = 46 — below the 150 line: no intrusion
Na = 95 — below the 150 line: no intrusion
Na = 180 — above the 150 line: seawater intrusion confirmed
Na = 180 — below the 150 line: no intrusion
Na = 120 — above the 150 line (that reading is Holualoa’s, not KEEI_B’s)
Na = 14 — below the 150 line: no intrusion

feedback.correct: Correct — noted in your field notebook: KEEI_B’s sodium is 180 mg/L, above 150 — with chloride over 250, that confirms seawater intrusion.
wrong: Keep only KEEI_B’s rows, then the one where the analyte is Na, and read that sodium value against 150.
Make sure you’re reading sodium (Na), not another analyte from the same well — KEEI_B has several, and only Na is the second marker.
With chloride already past 250, sodium clearing 150 is what confirms it — does KEEI_B’s sodium clear the line or not?

hotspots.label: A checklist clipped to the pump
hotspots.body: Why two markers? Chloride alone can climb for other reasons, so intrusion isn’t confirmed on chloride by itself. Sodium (Na) is the other dominant ion in seawater — when both chloride and sodium are elevated together at the same well, that co-signature is the diagnostic fingerprint of seawater reaching the aquifer. Chloride here has already crossed its line; the checklist says confirm it with the second marker before you touch the valve.

entry.title: Into the wellroom
entry.text: KEEI_B's chloride came back at 280 — well past the 250 line! Your colleague's warning rings in your ears: if the chloride's over 250, check the sodium levels at the same well. There's a hatch in the platform floor and a ladder dropping into the dark. You climb down into the wellroom beneath Ke‘ei — damp concrete, dripping pipes — and this is where you settle it: is KEEI_B's sodium high enough to confirm what the chloride is hinting at? Is seawater leaking into the well?

debrief.title: How this world worked
debrief.intro: This afternoon was one skill wearing a lab coat: take a big table of well readings, narrow it to the wells and analytes that matter, plot them, and test each reading against a line. String those moves together and a hidden saltwater intrusion gives itself away. Here is how each room was teaching that.
